name: The Tammesalu Oak

location.address: Kadriorg Park, the old oak grove (Tammesalu) in the naturalistic (vabakujunduslik) section, near Kirdetiik pond and the Japanese Garden

access: Free, public park, open at all times (same as the rest of Kadriorg Park)
transport: Tram 1 or 3 to the Kadriorg stop, then roughly a 10 to 12 minute walk through the park to the Japanese Garden / Kirdetiik area
verify_notes: Tallinn's thickest tree, standing in the surviving natural oak grove (Tammesalu) that Kadriorg Park's own naturalistic ('vabakujunduslik') section was built around in the 19th century (renovated from 1897 under landscape architect Georg Kuphaldt). Postimees interviewed Tallinn Botanic Garden dendrologist Olev Abner in 2017: he ranked it Tallinn's single thickest tree, girth 637 cm as measured in 2016, and noted it already had substantial girth in 1714 when Tsar Peter I bought the small manor and its surrounding oak grove that became Kadriorg -- i.e. the tree predates both Kadriorg Palace and the park itself. He described the grove as an 'imperial oak grove' (Kadrioru keiserlik tammik) that has been actively managed for centuries: branches cut back and young trees planted in to keep the density that let the oaks grow large and straight. A more recent, independent measurement in Loodusajakiri (Estonia's nature magazine), May 2024, put the same tree (described as standing 'Kirdetiik juures' / by the Northeast Pond, where isolated oaks survive from the earlier natural oak grove) at 6.48 m girth at breast height, ~22 m tall, branching at 1.7 m, 'in full vigour', and estimated it at 300-400 years old -- consistent growth from the 2016 figure (637 -> 648 cm over 8 years) and consistent ages, from two independent outlets eight years apart. Kadriorg Park's own official site (kadriorupark.ee) independently corroborates in its own words: 'the oak grove's northeastern part holds the park's thickest oak, girth 6.3 m', trees over 300 years old still standing there, and that the Japanese Garden sits on the seaward edge of this same grove. Location precision is approximate: none of the three sources give a GPS point for the individual trunk, only 'in the grove, northeastern part, by Kirdetiik' -- pin is centred near Kirdetiik pond/the Japanese Garden as the nearest fixed landmark; a future pass with a site visit or a geotagged photo could tighten this to confirmed. One minor discrepancy worth flagging for a later pass: Tallinn's own municipal register page (tallinn.ee/et/elurikkus/uksikobjektid) names a common horse chestnut (~612 cm) as the thickest among its individually REGISTERED (EELIS/KLO) protected objects; this oak does not appear to carry its own KLO register id, most likely because it sits inside a protected AREA (the park/grove) rather than being separately gazetted as a single object, so it does not contradict the register claim, it simply falls outside what that register counts.
